notes.meaning: Even though Israel had just won a great victory at Jericho, one man named Achan secretly took items that God had commanded to be completely destroyed. Because God treated the whole nation as one covenant family, Achan's hidden disobedience brought the Lord's anger down upon all of Israel.
Joshua sent scouts from Jericho up into the hills to examine the town of Ai, which lay near Bethel. Taking Ai was the next natural step to gain a foothold in the central hill country.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Archaeologists debate whether Ai was an occupied, fortified town during the late Bronze Age, leading some scholars to suggest it served as a smaller military outpost for Bethel.

notes.meaning: The scouts returned with high confidence and told Joshua that only two or three thousand soldiers were needed to capture Ai. They believed the town had very few fighters, so sending the whole army would only exhaust the men for no reason.

Joshua accepted their advice and sent about three thousand soldiers to attack Ai. However, instead of an easy triumph, the Israelite troops lost their courage when the defenders charged out, and they turned and ran.

The men of Ai chased the retreating soldiers down the rocky slopes and killed about thirty-six Israelites. Even though the loss of life was small, the defeat proved that Israel could be beaten, and the courage of the people melted away in fear.

Shocked by the defeat, Joshua and the elders tore their clothes and put dust on their heads as ancient signs of deep sorrow. They lay face down before the ark of the Lord until evening, realizing that without God's help they were helpless.

In his distress, Joshua cried out to God and asked why He had brought Israel across the Jordan only to let them be destroyed by the Amorites. His words showed human weakness and honest panic, even wondering aloud if they should have stayed on the east side of the river.
Joshua pleaded that he did not know what to say now that Israel had run from its enemies. The retreat had shaken their confidence and left their leader at a complete loss for words.

Joshua worried that the surrounding Canaanite nations would hear the news, join forces, and wipe Israel off the earth. Above all, he feared for God's honor, asking what God would do to defend His own great reputation among the nations if His people were destroyed.
The Lord ordered Joshua to get up from the ground and stop lying on his face. This was not the moment for prolonged weeping; decisive action was needed to deal with the wrongdoing in the camp.

God explained that Israel had broken the covenant by taking items devoted to destruction from Jericho. The offender had stolen what belonged exclusively to God, lied about the deed, and hidden the stolen plunder among personal goods.

God told Joshua that the army fled because bringing the forbidden goods into camp made Israel itself subject to destruction. The Lord warned that He would no longer remain with them unless they cleared out the devoted things completely.

Joshua was instructed to tell the people to consecrate themselves—to wash and spiritually prepare—for the next day. They had to understand that victory was impossible until the stolen goods were uncovered and judged.

The next morning, the people were to present themselves before the Lord group by group. God would guide the process—traditionally understood through casting sacred lots—to narrow the search from tribe to clan, family, and finally to the single guilty person.

The one found guilty was to be burned with fire along with everything that belonged to him. His theft was not just an ordinary crime; it was high treason against God's covenant and brought disgrace upon the entire community.
Joshua rose early in the morning to carry out God's orders without delay. He had the tribes step forward one by one, and the tribe of Judah was chosen.
Joshua then brought the clans of Judah forward, and the clan of the Zerahites was selected. When that clan was examined family by family, the family of Zabdi was singled out.

Finally, the family of Zabdi was brought forward individual by individual, and Achan was picked. This showed that no sin can remain hidden from God, no matter how carefully someone tries to conceal it.

Joshua spoke with gentle concern, calling Achan his son and urging him to give glory to God by telling the whole truth. Confessing sin honors God by acknowledging that He knows all secrets and judges justly.
Achan admitted his guilt openly and gave a straightforward confession. He made no excuses and confessed that he had sinned directly against the Lord, the God of Israel.

Achan described the steps that led to his fall: he looked at a luxurious imported robe from Babylon and a pile of silver and gold, felt intense desire for them, and took them. He then buried the stolen goods deep under the dirt floor of his tent.
Joshua immediately dispatched messengers who ran to the tent to confirm the story. They searched the ground inside and found the items buried exactly where Achan said they would be.

The messengers dug up the stolen goods, carried them back to Joshua and the assembled elders, and spread them out before the Lord. Laying the plunder before God showed that the hidden crime had been fully uncovered.

Joshua and the whole community took Achan, the stolen goods, his family, and all his animals and belongings to a nearby valley. Because the devoted items had contaminated his entire household, everything connected with him had to be taken outside the camp.

Joshua asked Achan why he had brought ruin upon Israel, declaring that the Lord would bring trouble upon him that very day. The people executed Achan by stoning and burned his remains and possessions with fire to purge the wickedness from among them.

differ.view: Some hold that only Achan was put to death, while his children were brought out only to watch the punishment and take warning, because the law forbade killing children for their parents' sins.
Many hold that Achan's children were executed with him because they likely helped conceal the stolen goods in the tent and shared in the guilt of the devoted things.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary notes that Achan was executed along with his children and herds under the total ban placed upon Jericho.

notes.meaning: The people piled a large mound of stones over the site as a lasting monument and warning against covetous disobedience. Once the sin was judged, the Lord's anger ceased, and the place was named the Valley of Achor, which means the Valley of Trouble.
